description: LunaTabula is a team of passionate innovators exploring new possibilities in lunar exploration. Through NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to develop an innovative and practical solution for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by combining scientific thinking, creativity, research, and technology. Our goal is to make lunar site exploration and navigation smarter, safer, and more efficient, contributing to the future of human exploration beyond Earth.
summary:
We developed Lunar Site Navigator, an interactive decision-support web application designed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to help mission planners and researchers evaluate candidate lunar south-polar regions.
​What we built: A live, responsive web tool that integrates official NASA Artemis III candidate regions, 360° local terrain horizon profiles, and topocentric Sun/Earth ephemeris geometry.
​How it addresses the challenge: It translates complex ephemeris data into intuitive visualizations, letting users scrub UTC timelines, view Sun and Earth sky-paths against local crater rims, and instantly identify mission risks. Crucially, it strictly separates geometric visibility from terrain line-of-sight and enforces data verification badges (VERIFIED, PROVISIONAL, ILLUSTRATIVE) to prevent scientific overreach.
​Why it is important: Safe lunar exploration depends on continuous power and communication. Our tool provides transparent, reproducible mission intelligence required for sustainable Artemis exploration.
details: Lunar Site Navigator is an interactive decision-support web application built to help mission planners, researchers, and students evaluate candidate lunar south-polar landing sites for the Artemis era. Users select from NASA's nine official Artemis III candidate regions, scrub through UTC timelines, and explore interactive 360° azimuth-elevation horizon plots. The application compares real-time Sun and Earth sky trajectories against local digital elevation model (DEM) terrain silhouettes to determine solar illumination availability and direct-to-Earth line-of-sight.
